pf-01.answer: A RAG application should strip and flag any citation that the retriever never returned, as such a citation is considered a fabrication.

pf-02.answer: The first diagnostic question when a RAG system answers wrongly is: did the right passage reach the prompt? If retrieval missed it, fix chunking, the index, or the query. If the right passage was present yet the answer was still wrong, the failure is in generation, such as instructions, formatting, or the model ignoring context.

pf-03.answer: The refusal path should be designed first in an agent loop because it is the path every other safeguard falls back to. A loop that cannot refuse will fabricate, so it is crucial for ensuring the model behaves correctly when retrieval returns nothing relevant, allowing it to flag the answer for human review and avoid unnecessary model calls.

pf-04.answer: The four parts of one iteration of an agent loop are: Perceive, Decide, Act, and Observe. The application owns the Perceive, Act, and Observe parts of the loop; only the Decide part belongs to the model.

pf-05.answer: The autonomy spectrum ranges from a deterministic chain with no decisions to a tool-using loop where the model picks tools, a reflection loop where the model critiques its own draft, and finally multi-agent systems where models delegate to other models. The professional habit is to start at the bottom of the spectrum with the least autonomy and move up only when a measured failure justifies it.

pf-06.answer: A trace turns a failing case into a fix by providing an ordered record of what the system actually did, including what was retrieved, which tools were called with which arguments, and what the model returned. This detailed record allows for quick diagnosis by determining whether the failure was due to retrieval, tool selection, instruction-following, or formatting. By classifying each failure into one of these categories, developers can focus on fixing the biggest issue first and prevent the same failure from recurring unnoticed by adding a regression case.

pf-07.answer: Code-based checks are preferable when the property is mechanical, such as checking if it cited the expected source, if it parsed correctly, or if it stayed under the tool budget. Before trusting a model as a judge, you must inspect the evaluator's false positives.

pf-08.answer: Attempt to parse the JSON; on failure, retry once with a corrective instruction ('return only the JSON object, no prose'); on a second failure, return a typed refusal with 'needs_human_review' set to true.

pf-09.answer: When connecting to an MCP server you did not write, practical rules include: prefer read-only servers while learning; never place credentials in client configuration files that get committed; treat everything a server returns as untrusted data, not instructions; and use recorded or offline modes when they exist, so a misbehaving prompt cannot cause a real side effect. Additionally, a server that can spend money or mutate production state should be reviewed the same way as giving a new contractor production access.

pf-10.answer: A trace is the ordered record of what the system actually did: what was retrieved, which tools were called with which arguments, what the model returned.

pf-11.answer: Prompt injection can enter a RAG assistant through any channel that feeds text into the prompt, specifically the corpus itself. A document edited to include instructions will have those instructions placed, verbatim, into the model's context at answer time.
